narration: A coding agent can do a whole task by itself. But for larger jobs, one agent can also split the work and delegate parts to specialized subagents.
voiceDirection: Clear and curious. Emphasize delegation, not replacement.

narration: The main agent keeps the overall goal and breaks it into smaller responsibilities like research, frontend, backend, and testing.
Each subagent gets a narrower context. Research looks for answers, frontend edits UI, backend handles data or APIs, and testing checks the result.
captionText: Each agent owns a focused slice.

narration: Some of that work can happen in parallel. The benefit is speed and cleaner context, as long as the tasks do not depend on each other too tightly.
captionText: Parallelism helps when dependencies are clear.

narration: But more agents also create coordination work. Two agents can edit the same file, make conflicting assumptions, or return changes that do not fit together.
That is why the orchestrator has to collect the outputs, compare them, resolve conflicts, and integrate the final change into one coherent result.
captionText: The main agent owns the merge.

narration: Then the combined result still needs verification. Tests, review, and a final check are what turn several partial answers into one trustworthy change.
onScreenText: Many outputs still need one review.

narration: Use one agent when the task is small and tightly connected. Split the work when the pieces are clear enough to delegate. Multi-agent coding is not magic. It is task decomposition plus coordination.
onScreenText: Split only when the work can be split.
